RESOLVED 2026-09-19: the flagged sentence ('Nothing in this provision limits Tenant's statutory right to cure nonpayment') was corrected at the source -- softened to 'any statutory right Tenant may have,' a uniform fix applied to the shared clause across all 8 tagged states, not an Ohio-only override. Ohio genuinely has no statutory cure right (R.C. 1923.04 is a notice to leave, not a pay-or-quit); the same defect had already been separately flagged for South Dakota in CO's own citation note and was never fixed until now.

R.C. 5321.01(E) defines a security deposit broadly as any deposit of money or property to secure performance -- prepaid last month's rent listed in this fill-in-the-blank clause likely falls inside that definition (interest under 5321.16(A), return/itemization under (B)). Interpretive, not a defect in the clause's own text -- flagged as background for whoever fills in the bracketed amounts on an Ohio lease, not a citation gap.

Ohio has no statutory returned-check fee cap that binds a landlord. The $30-or-10% figure quoted in many Ohio lease templates is R.C. 1319.16, which caps what a COLLECTION AGENCY may charge; R.C. 1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting on its own account. The clause's existing self-limiting language ('not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law') correctly resolves to 'no fixed cap, state an actual amount' for Ohio, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability as the only ceiling -- same self-limiting pattern already used for `holdover`, working as intended here.

No Ohio conflict with the clause's early-termination fee mechanics, but the greater-of-one-month-or-30% fee carries real R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability exposure in Ohio specifically, and Ohio's own mitigation-of-damages duty (Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone, a COMMERCIAL holding not yet tested residentially) is itself waivable -- do not stack a mitigation waiver on top of this fee for an Ohio lease. Risk-awareness note, not a stated defect in the shipped bodyText.

R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of ch. 5321 non-waivable and (E) bars receipt of rent free of 5321.04 habitability compliance. The clause's move-in condition acknowledgment must be read as a statement of fact about the property's condition, not a waiver of the landlord's continuing habitability duty -- an interpretive caution about how to use the existing language, not a defect requiring the bodyText to change.

Ohio has NO abandoned-property disposal procedure for a conventional residential tenancy -- the notice/valuation/county-auditor/sale machinery at R.C. 1923.12-.14 applies only to manufactured-home parks, and R.C. 5321.15(B) separately bars seizing a tenant's possessions for rent except by court order. The clause's existing self-limiting language ('to the extent permitted by applicable law') correctly resolves to 'very little to no disposal right' for Ohio, same self-limiting pattern as `returned-payments`/`holdover` -- see the companion `edu-no-abandoned-property-safe-harbor-oh` education row for the full landlord-facing explanation.

R.C. 5321.04(A)(8): reasonable notice required, with 24 hours presumed reasonable absent contrary evidence; entry only at reasonable times. Remedies at (B): actual damages, injunction, statutory attorney's fees, or termination. R.C. 5321.05(B): tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to entry. The clause's own built-in 24-hour figure matches Ohio's presumed-reasonable standard directly, the same reason Nebraska's fixed 24-hour rule let this clause extend to NE without an override. Effective 1974-11-04 (SB 103, 110th GA), never amended. A REWRITE of the pre-existing, never-audited row (Taylor's explicit decision 2026-09-18), not a repair -- the prior text had five defects: interest promised on the whole deposit rather than only the excess over the greater of $50 or one month's rent; keyed to lease term rather than duration of possession; '6 months' misstated against the statutory 'six months or more'; the 5% rate left unstated; the annual computation-and-payment duty omitted. Whether a failure to pay (A) interest triggers (C)'s double-damages-plus-fees remedy (keyed to a failure of (B)) is unsettled -- mooted by drafting the clause to pay correctly rather than relying on the reading.

Two conjunctive triggers -- termination AND delivery of possession -- unlike MN/SD, which key the clock to receipt of the tenant's forwarding address. (B)'s final sentence is the statute's own landlord protection: a tenant who fails to furnish a forwarding address in writing forfeits the (C) remedy (damages plus attorney's fees) while the landlord keeps the deposit itself. (C)'s remedy is the money due plus damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees -- nets to double, but the statute never uses the word 'double' and provides no treble damages.

citation: R.C. ch. 5321 (confirmed no holdover formula); R.C. 1923.02(A)(1); R.C. 1923.081
notes: The generic `holdover` clause promises 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' -- Ohio has NO holdover-damages formula at all, confirmed on full-chapter primary reads of both ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 (2026-09-18). §1923.02(A)(1) makes holding over a possession ground; §1923.081 permits joining a rent/damages claim 'under a rental agreement.' Holdover damages in Ohio are therefore purely contractual, so the override requires a landlord-set `{{holdover_daily_rate}}` or the clause promises nothing -- same failure mode as South Dakota's `holdover-sd`, different underlying cause (SD repealed its own rule; Ohio never had one). §5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling on the stated rate. Deliberately omits an 'acceptance does not create a new tenancy' sentence, since accepting rent for a FUTURE period after an R.C. 1923.04 notice waives the notice as a matter of law regardless of lease language (see `edu-waiver-by-acceptance-oh`).

R.C. 5321.13(D) bars any tenant agreement to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law. Unlike K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4), Ohio's ban carries NO common-areas exception, so dropping the parent clause's liability-limiting sentence entirely is required for Ohio, not merely prudent. Every written rental agreement shall contain the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent; for an oral tenancy the same information must be given in writing at commencement. Fourth distinct sanction architecture found across this project's 7 prior states: Ohio does not make the non-discloser an implied agent (KS's approach), or the landlord (NE's), or impose a maintenance bar (MN's) -- under 5321.18(C), failure WAIVES the landlord's right to receive the tenant's 5321.07/5321.08 notices, so the tenant may proceed without giving the landlord the usual repair-notice opportunity.

New topic -- no other state in this library has a flag-display row. (A) bars any rental-agreement restriction on display of the US flag, the state flag, a service flag, or a POW/MIA flag. Scope correction from an initial draft: the (B) notice-and-consultation duty applies only to a flag POLE or a permanently affixed BRACKET, and only for the US and POW/MIA flags specifically -- it does not attach to the state flag or service flag limbs, and not to ordinary (non-permanent) display.

Two-limb conjunctive exemption from the tenant's repair-and-escrow remedy: the landlord must both (a) be party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units, and (b) give WRITTEN NOTICE of that fact. The disclosure is a condition precedent -- the exemption simply fails without it, so this clause should only be included where limb (a) is actually true (a factual representation, not boilerplate). Ohio has four different portfolio thresholds across four separate provisions -- none (ch. 4112 fair housing), three-or-fewer (5321.07(C)), fewer-than-four (1923.062(C)), four-or-more (5321.04(A)(5)) -- see `edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh`.

Conjunctive two-part test: registry listing under the registry maintained at R.C. 2950.13 AND a qualifying offense -- both limbs required, a bare registry hit alone is not enough. Termination under (A)(2) reaches the tenant and all other occupants, and is also triggered where a person establishes residence in violation of R.C. 2950.031. (B) shields the landlord: a landlord authorized to act under this section is protected from a resulting claim by the terminated tenant.

R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of ch. 5321 non-waivable except through (F), and (F) permits only one move: the landlord assuming the tenant's 5321.05 duties. There is no route in the other direction. Inverse of the KS/ND/NE structured-delegation architecture, where duty-shifting runs toward the tenant under conditions -- do not import those states' delegation clauses into Ohio. Resolves the named-topic checklist's 'is that duty waivable' question for Ohio: no, and uniquely one-directional among the 8 states in this library.

Chain verified section-open 2026-09-18: 5321.05(A)(9) is the tenant's duty not to engage in drug-related activity; 5321.05(A)(2) directs the landlord to 'promptly' give the 5321.17(C) notice; 5321.17(C) states the tenancy terminates three days after the notice regardless of any charge, plea, or conviction; if the tenant does not vacate, the landlord 'promptly shall comply with' 5321.04(A)(9). §1923.051 provides an accelerated eviction track (service within 3 working days, trial within 30 days, no continuances) -- unlike most Ohio eviction grounds, this one is framed as close to mandatory for the landlord once actual knowledge or reasonable cause exists, not merely discretionary.

Added by SB 237 (135th GA), effective 2025-04-09 -- recent enough that older Ohio landlord guidance is unlikely to reflect it. If a minor tenant is named as a defendant on an eviction complaint alongside a parent or adult guardian, the court SHALL dismiss the action without prejudice and SHALL order the landlord to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorney's fees. The same act added a two-year limitations period for FED actions at 1923.01(B). Flagged as a hard validation rule for any future eviction-filing or occupant-list feature, not just a background education note.

If the Ohio Civil Rights Commission issues a housing discrimination complaint, either party (not just the complainant) may elect to move the matter into common pleas court. Current 4112.055 is effective 2025-09-30, amended by HB 96 (136th GA) -- the biennial BUDGET bill, one of several instances this project found of Ohio moving fair-housing/landlord-tenant law through appropriations acts rather than dedicated bills. Filing windows: one year for a commission charge (4112.05(B)(1)) AND one year for a private civil action (4112.055(A)(1)) -- the two-year figure sometimes cited is the EMPLOYMENT window at 4112.051 and does not apply to housing.

Confirmed absent from the ORC on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary-source agreement for the rest of the Code -- there is no direct Ohio smoke- or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute for rentals. The duty reaches landlords indirectly: 5321.04(A)(1) requires compliance with applicable building/housing/health/safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and 5321.19(B)(1) preserves local codes from ch. 5321 preemption. Different architecture from Nebraska (Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-5,144) and North Dakota (N.D.C.C. 23-13-15), both of which have a direct statutory duty -- do not adapt those states' rows to Ohio. No agreement to pay the landlord's OR the tenant's attorney's fees is recognized in a residential rental agreement, or in any OTHER agreement between a landlord and tenant. Broader than K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) and Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1415(1)(c) because of the final limb reaching any other agreement, not just the lease -- this is the finding that drives withholding the generic `default-by-tenant` from Ohio in favor of `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`.

Ohio gives landlords no statutory returned-check fee cap -- the commonly-quoted $30-or-10% figure is R.C. 1319.16, a collection-agency cap that 1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account from. A tenant gets two independent cure windows before any bad-check exposure attaches: 2913.11(C)(2)'s 10-day cure (the presumption of knowledge fails if liability is discharged within 10 days of a dishonor notice) and 2307.61(D)'s 30-day cure (payment within 30 days of a written demand bars the civil action entirely). 2307.61(H)(2)(b) includes the landlord's own bank NSF charge inside the 'value' figure that gets trebled under (A)(1)(b). 2913.11(A)(1)(b) defines 'check' to include ACH and card transactions, so a failed electronic rent payment is inside this framework too.

citation: King v. Dolton, 9th Dist. No. 02CA0041, 2003-Ohio-2423; Bristol Court v. Jones (4th Dist. 1994); N. Face Properties v. Lin, 2013-Ohio-2281 (12th Dist.); OZ Property Mgt. v. Williams, 2025-Ohio-318 (12th Dist.); Premiere Mgt. v. Nutt, 2010-Ohio-1255 (3d Dist.)
notes: Case law, not statute. The line is temporal: accepting rent for obligations already incurred at the time of a §1923.04 three-day notice does not waive it (King v. Dolton, citing Sholiton Indus. v. Royal Arms); accepting rent for a FUTURE period after the notice waives it as a matter of law and the landlord cannot proceed on it (Bristol Court v. Jones). A landlord 'accepts' by cashing OR by silently holding a payment without telling the tenant it isn't accepted (N. Face Properties v. Lin, citing Associated Estates Corp. v. Bartell). Risk starts earlier than the notice itself: accepting current-month rent BEFORE serving the notice can jeopardize the right to immediate restitution (OZ Property Mgt. v. Williams). Five appellate districts (2d, 3d, 4th, 9th, 12th) agree -- statewide consensus, not district variation.

citation: Castlebrook, Ltd. v. Dayton Properties Ltd. Partnership, 78 Ohio App.3d 340, 348 (2d Dist. 1992); Tuteur v. P. & F. Enterprises, Inc., 21 Ohio App.2d 122, 133 (8th Dist. 1970); Grisham v. Meadow Ridge Cincinnati Assocs. (12th Dist.)
notes: Case law, not statute. Ohio has no statute transferring deposit liability to a buyer on sale and no safe harbor for doing it properly. A security deposit is a personal obligation in the nature of a PLEDGE, not part of the property's 'rent, issues, and profits' -- liability to return it stays with the original landlord (the pledgee) unless the buyer either assumes the obligation or receives a credit on the purchase price for the deposits (Castlebrook, quoting Tuteur, which adopted the New Jersey pledge rule because no Ohio authority existed in 1970). Grisham applied the same rule where a PET deposit's inclusion turned on whether it fell inside the purchase agreement's own 'Tenant Deposit' definition. Practical consequence for the product: an Ohio seller who wants out of deposit liability must actually move the money and notify the tenant in writing naming the successor holder -- this is a real ownership-transfer workflow question, not just a lease-clause one.

Confirmed absent on full-chapter primary reads of both ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 (2026-09-18). The detailed notice/valuation/county-auditor/sale machinery at 1923.12-.14 applies only to manufactured-home parks; 5321.15(B) separately bars seizing a tenant's possessions for rent except by court order. There is also no post-writ duty regarding a tenant's PET left behind -- a gap worth flagging separately, since none of the eviction-duty screen rows cover it either. One secondary commercial-vendor source states 'no statute' for Ohio on this point and happens to be right, but that conclusion was independently confirmed here from the primary chapters, not adopted from the vendor.

There is no general 'small landlord' concept in Ohio law -- four separate provisions use four different portfolio tests. Fair housing under ch. 4112 has NO small-landlord exemption at all (4112.024's exemption list contains no portfolio test, and 4112.01(A)(1)'s definition of 'person' sweeps in any owner, lessor, manager, or agent) -- a real contrast with Kansas, which exempts a small landlord from fair housing entirely (K.S.A. 44-1018(b)). The other three thresholds: 3-or-fewer units (5321.07(C), the repair-escrow exemption), fewer-than-4 (1923.062(C), the state SCRA analog), and 4-or-more (5321.04(A)(5), the waste-receptacle duty). Caveat: only 4112.01 and 4112.024 were read in full; the rest of ch. 4112 was not, so an exemption elsewhere in that chapter hasn't been fully ruled out.

Bundled absence finding, confirmed on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary agreement across the rest of the Code: no security deposit cap, no late fee cap, no returned-check fee cap that binds a landlord, no holdover damages formula, and no required mold, radon, bed bug, meth, asbestos, or flood disclosure. The lone mandated lease disclosure is owner/agent identity (5321.18). The commonly-cited $50-or-one-month figure in 5321.16 is the INTEREST THRESHOLD, not a deposit cap -- a widely misreported distinction. R.C. 5302.30 is a SALES disclosure form and does not apply to rentals -- the most likely trap on an 'Ohio disclosure requirements' search. Pending but NOT enacted: HB 841 (introduced 2026-04-30) would create a mold/lead/radon/CO awareness PROGRAM, and would not itself create a disclosure duty even if it passes.

Confirmed absent on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 -- there is no rent-increase notice provision at all. The '30 days' figure widely quoted for Ohio is 5321.17(B), the notice required to TERMINATE a month-to-month tenancy, not a rent-increase rule -- the practical route to a higher rent on a periodic tenancy is to terminate and offer a new one at the new rate. Same error shape already found once in this project's Nebraska research (a termination-notice period misreported as a rent-increase rule).

citation: R.C. 5301.11; Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone, 99 Ohio St.3d 254, 2003-Ohio-3648
notes: R.C. 5301.11 (Title 53, ch. 5301 Conveyances -- an adjacent-title find invisible to a ch. 5321-only read; effective 1953-10-01, sole version, unamended): a tenant whose building is destroyed or rendered unfit for occupancy without their fault is relieved of rent obligations after the destruction, UNLESS otherwise expressly provided by written agreement, and must then surrender possession. Because this sits outside ch. 5321, R.C. 5321.13(A)'s non-waivability does NOT protect it -- an Ohio lease can contract around it, subject only to 5321.14 unconscionability. Separately, Lemstone's mitigation-of-damages holding is expressly limited to a COMMERCIAL lease (the Ohio Supreme Court said so in framing the issue), and every decision upholding a mitigation waiver in Ohio is commercial -- whether a RESIDENTIAL mitigation waiver survives 5321.14 is genuinely untested. PARTIAL because both citations are solid on their own terms, but the residential-application question for each is an open, undecided legal question, not a citation gap that more reading would close. Taylor's decision 2026-09-18: no mitigation waiver in the default Ohio lease; surface both points in landlord education as available-but-untested rather than building either into shipped clause text.

Built 2026-09-19 to close the gap this citation-extraction pass surfaced -- Ohio was the only one of the 7 prior states with no assistance-animal-accommodation override, despite Ohio's own canvass (items #61/#62/#74/#127/#128/#129) already confirming OAC 4112-5-07(C)'s no-extra-charge duty. Also independently grounded in the federal Fair Housing Act (24 C.F.R. §100.204, the same regulation this project's Kansas legal-watch already monitors). Deliberately omits a Colorado-style criminal-misrepresentation-penalty sentence (Ohio's §§955.011/955.43 confirmed to contain no such offense for private housing, canvass item #39) and does not overspecify a documentation-verification procedure (Ohio has none, canvass items #74/#127) -- the clause's existing self-limiting language is the correct level of specificity for Ohio, not an omission.
